extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of poetics; poets and dramatists studying Aristotle's rules for epic and tragic composition
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and criticising epic and tragic poetry, emphasizing plot construction, diction, metre, modes of imitation, and how to handle the improbable or irrational in verse. Draws on Aristotle's Poetics with examples and critical tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command of metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest thing by far is to have a command of metaphor; to make good metaphors implies an eye for resemblances and is the mark of genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor cannot be imparted by another; it distinguishes style. Value metaphoric faculty highly when judging poetic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety in modes of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe propriety in several modes of expression—compound words, strange (or rare) words, and so forth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate use of compound and rare words gives distinction; excessive or misplaced rarity can harm clarity. Use according to the demands of metre and genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of diction by genre and metre
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the various kinds of words, the compound are best adapted to dithyrambs, rare words to heroic poetry, metaphors to iambic; in heroic poetry all varieties are serviceable; in iambic verse the most appropriate words are those found even in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match lexical variety to subgenre: heroic (heroic/epic) can sustain rare words and metaphors; iambic aims to reproduce familiar speech and should favour current/proper, metaphorical, and ornamental words as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot unity and completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot ought to be constructed on dramatic principles: it should have for its subject a single action, whole and complete, with a beginning, a middle, and an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A coherent single action produces the pleasure proper to imitation; avoid over-vast themes that cannot be embraced in a single view. Use episodes sparingly so they serve the single action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish epic narrative from historical sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic differs from historical compositions: epics present a single action (or portion) rather than a mere sequence of events within a period that do not tend to one result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing an epic, detach a single portion of a larger material and admit episodes that diversify but still contribute to overall unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds and parts required in epic (reversals, recognitions, incidents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry must have as many kinds as Tragedy (simple, complex, ethical, pathetic); its parts, except song and scenery, are the same and it requires Reversals, Recognitions, and Tragic Incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate epics on presence and artful handling of these structural moments; thoughts and diction must also be artistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and limits of epic
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning and the end must be capable of being brought within a single view; poems should be of a scale answering in length to the group of tragedies presented at one sitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid themes too vast to be apprehended as a whole; maintain a manageable scale that preserves unity while permitting grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic's capacity for multiple simultaneous events
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the narrative form, epic can present many events simultaneously transacted if relevant, which add mass and dignity and relieve sameness by varying episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concurrent events and episodes to build grandeur, provided they remain relevant to the subject and do not undermine unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate metre choice
rubrics_metrics.description: The heroic measure (epic metre) is the stateliest and most massive and thus most fitting for large-scale narrative poetry; mixing metres is absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select metre by nature of imitation: heroic for epic; iambic and trochaic tetrameter for more stirring or dance-like effects; avoid inconsistent mixing (example: Chaeremon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's self-presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should speak as little as possible in his own person; imitation is not achieved by the poet's personal intrusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let characters and their actions speak; use minimal authorial comment. Homer is praised for bringing in characters quickly and letting them display characteristic qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admit the wonderful but prefer probable impossibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of the wonderful is admissible and pleasing; the poet should prefer probable impossibilities to improbable possibilities—the tragic plot must not be composed of irrational parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the 'irrational' is introduced, it should be made probable or lie outside the action of the play; absurdities inside the drama are intolerable unless veilable by poetic charm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude irrational incidents from the action
rubrics_metrics.description: Irrational incidents should, if possible, be excluded; if tolerated they should lie outside the action (e.g., hero's ignorance) and not internal contradictions within the drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticisms that a plot would be ruined by excluding an incident are weak; construct plots to avoid reliance on irreconcilable irrationalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction timing and moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: The diction should be elaborated in the pauses of the action, where there is no expression of character or thought; conversely, character and thought are obscured by a diction that is over-brilliant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ornate diction during non-character moments; keep speech clear and appropriate during expression of character and thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three objects of imitation and vehicles of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet must imitate one of three objects—things as they were or are, things as they are said or thought to be, or things as they ought to be; vehicles of expression are language—current terms, rare words, or metaphors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge correctness relative to the chosen object of imitation and vehicle; standards of correctness vary between poetry and other arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate essential faults from accidental faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Within poetry there are faults that touch its essence (inherent to the imitation) and those that are accidental (errors about the represented matter, e.g., technical inaccuracy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential faults are more serious; accidental errors (e.g., factual slips about an art) are less destructive of poetic value unless they impair the poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify impossible elements by artistic ends
rubrics_metrics.description: If the poet has represented things impossible according to the laws of an art, the error may be justified if the artistic end (poetic effect) is thereby better attained; otherwise avoid the error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the impossibility was necessary for effect; if the same end could be achieved without violating rules, the violation is unjustified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual evaluation of acts and sayings
rubrics_metrics.description: In judging whether a saying or act is poetically right, consider by whom it is said or done, to whom, when, in whose interest, and for what end—not merely the isolated act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate utterances and actions within dramatic context and motivation rather than in abstraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive methods for critical difficulties
rubrics_metrics.description: Many critical difficulties may be resolved by reference to accent, breathing, punctuation, ambiguity of construction, or the usage of language; words may be metaphorical or have multiple senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before condemning a passage as erroneous, test alternative readings (accentuation, punctuation, ambiguity, usage, dialectal senses) and consider received usages and metaphorical senses (examples given from Homer and others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject groundless critical leaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics often jump to groundless conclusions, pass adverse judgment, and then reason from that assumption; interpretation should avoid such fallacies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek plausible alternate historical or dialectal explanations (e.g., variations in local traditions) rather than assuming error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five sources of critical objection
rubrics_metrics.description: Things are censured either as impossible, irrational, morally hurtful, contradictory, or contrary to artistic correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When responding to criticism, address objections under these five heads and use the twelve interpretive/analytic methods mentioned earlier to justify or correct the poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary depravity of character
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of depravity of character is justly censured when there is no inner necessity for introducing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce immoral or depraved traits only when essential to the plot or artistic aim; otherwise such traits are proper grounds for censure (examples: Aegeus in Euripides, Menelaus in the Orestes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference of refined art for cultivated audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: If the more refined art is higher, Epic (which appeals to a cultivated audience and requires less gesture) is superior to Tragedy (addressed to an inferior public and more unrefined).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the level of refinement of imitation and the intended audience when judging comparative merit between modes (epic vs tragic).
